text:
Mademoiselle Georges looked sternly and gloomily over the audience and began to recite in French some verses that spoke of her criminal love for her son. At times she raised her voice, at times she whispered, solemnly lifting her head; at times she paused and rasped, rolling her eyes.

“Adorable, divine, delicious!” was heard on all sides.

Natasha looked at the stout Georges, but heard nothing, saw nothing, and understood nothing of what was taking place before her; she only felt herself once again wholly and irrevocably in that strange, mad world, so remote from her former world, in that world in which it was impossible to know what was good, what was bad, what was reasonable, and what was mad. Anatole was sitting behind her, and, feeling his nearness, she waited fearfully for something.

After the first monologue, the whole company rose and surrounded Mademoiselle Georges, expressing their delight to her.

“How good she is!” Natasha said to her father, who had risen with the others and was making his way through the crowd toward the actress.

“I do not think so, looking at you,” said Anatole, following Natasha. He said this at a moment when she alone could hear him. “You are enchanting... From the moment I saw you, I have not ceased...”

“Come, come, Natasha,” said the count, returning for his daughter. “How good she is!”

Without saying anything, Natasha went up to her father and looked at him with questioning, astonished eyes.

After several more recitations, Mademoiselle Georges left, and Countess Bezukhov asked the company to go into the ballroom.

The count wanted to leave, but Hélène begged him not to spoil her improvised ball. The Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha to waltz, and during the waltz, as he pressed her waist and hand, he told her that she was ravishing and that he loved her. During the écossaise, which she again danced with Kuragin, when they were alone, Anatole said nothing to her and merely looked at her. Natasha was in doubt as to whether she had dreamed what he had said to her during the waltz. At the end of the first figure, he pressed her hand again. Natasha raised frightened eyes to him, but there was such a self-assuredly tender expression in his affectionate gaze and smile that, looking at him, she could not say what she had meant to say to him. She lowered her eyes.

“Do not say such things to me; I am engaged and I love another,” she said quickly... She glanced at him. Anatole was neither disconcerted nor distressed by what she had said.

“Do not speak to me about that. What do I care?” he said. “I tell you that I am madly, madly in love with you. Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... We must begin.”

Animated and anxious, Natasha looked around her with wide-open, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She remembered almost nothing of what happened that evening. They danced the écossaise and the Grossvater; her father asked her to leave, and she begged to stay. Wherever she was and whoever she spoke to, she felt his gaze upon her. Later she remembered that she had asked her father’s permission to go to the dressing room to straighten her dress, that Hélène had followed her, laughing as she spoke to her about her brother’s love, and that in the small sitting room she had met Anatole again, that Hélène had disappeared somewhere, that they had been left alone, and that Anatole, taking her hand, had said in a tender voice:

“I cannot visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Never?...” And, blocking her way, he brought his face closer to hers.

His large, shining, masculine eyes were so close to her eyes that she saw nothing but those eyes.

“Natalie?!” his voice whispered questioningly, and someone was painfully squeezing her hands. “Natalie?!”

“I understand nothing; I have nothing to say,” said her gaze.

Hot lips pressed against her lips, and at that same moment she felt herself free again, and the sound of Hélène’s footsteps and rustling dress was heard in the room. Natasha looked around at Hélène, then, red and trembling, looked at him fearfully and questioningly and went toward the door.

“One word, just one, in God’s name,” Anatole was saying.

She stopped. She so needed him to say that word which would explain to her what had happened and to which she would give him an answer.

“Nathalie, one word, just one,” he kept repeating, evidently not knowing what to say, and he repeated it until Hélène came up to them.

Hélène and Natasha returned to the drawing room together. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

After returning home, Natasha did not sleep all night: she was tormented by the insoluble question of whom she loved, Anatole or Prince Andrei. She loved Prince Andrei—she clearly remembered how strongly she loved him. But she loved Anatole too; that was beyond doubt. “Otherwise, could all this have happened?” she thought. “If, after this, when saying good-bye to him, I could answer his smile with a smile, if I could allow it to come to this, it means that I loved him from the first moment. It means that he is kind, noble, and splendid, and it was impossible not to love him. What am I to do when I love him and love another?” she said to herself, finding no answers to these terrible questions.

XIV.

Morning came with its cares and bustle. Everyone got up, began moving about and talking; the dressmakers came again, Marya Dmitrievna appeared again, and they were called to tea. With her eyes wide open, as though she wished to intercept every gaze directed at her, Natasha looked uneasily at everyone and tried to seem just as she had always been.

After breakfast, Marya Dmitrievna—this was her best time—sat down in her armchair and called Natasha and the old count over to her.

“Well now, my friends, I have thought the whole matter over, and here is my advice,” she began. “Yesterday, as you know, I went to Prince Nikolai; well, and I talked to him... He took it into his head to shout. But he cannot outshout me! I told him everything!”

“But what did he say?” asked the count.

“What did he say? The madcap... He will not listen; but what is the use of talking? As it is, we have tormented the poor girl enough,” said Marya Dmitrievna. “And my advice to you is to finish your business and go home, to Otradnoe... and wait there...”

“Oh, no!” Natasha cried out.

“No, you must go,” said Marya Dmitrievna. “And wait there. If the bridegroom comes here now, there is bound to be a quarrel; but there, alone with the old man, he will discuss everything, and then he will come to you.”

Ilya Andreyevich approved of this proposal, immediately understanding all its reasonableness. If the old man softened, it would be all the better to visit him in Moscow or at Bald Hills afterward; if not, they could marry against his will only at Otradnoe.
